question: Is it permissible to play the Qur'an in the background while driving or doing chores?
asked: A sister listens to the Qur'an as much as she can while driving and at home, but she came across a verse saying that when the Qur'an is recited, one must stop everything and listen attentively. Is it permissible to have the Qur'an playing in the background while she drives or does housework and might not be actively listening? Is she sinful for this?
answer:
The verse that our sister Zahra from Leicester... By the way, when I used to go to England frequently, in the beginning I would say it the way it's spelled, and I made a big embarrassment of myself when I visited the city and I mispronounced the name, because it's spelled Leicester, but it is pronounced "Lester." So from the city of Leicester, she emails and she asks about this verse in the Qur'an.

The verse that she is referencing is Surat al-A'raf, verse 204. Surat al-A'raf, verse 204, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says: "When the Qur'an is recited, then pay attention to it and be quiet, so that you may achieve Allah's mercy." So this verse here gives us the ideal situation, the ideal scenario, and that is that when the Qur'an is played, you should pay attention to it. Istima' means to pay full attention. Ansitu means that you be quiet, and you are not doing something that's going to be against the fact that you're paying full attention, so that you may achieve Allah's mercy.

Now, this verse tells us the ideal, and the ideal is that you listen to the Qur'an as an action of worship. Because realize, when it comes to the Qur'an there are two separate actions: number one, reciting; number two, listening. It is authentically reported that our Prophet ﷺ asked Ubayy ibn Ka'b to recite the Qur'an to him. And Ubayy said, "O Messenger of Allah, do you want me to recite the Qur'an to you, and it was revealed to you?" And he said, "Yes, because I love to listen to its recitation as well." So to recite the Qur'an is an act of worship; to listen to its recitation is an act of worship. Therefore, the ideal is that you listen to the Qur'an as an action of worship.

Now the question arises: are you allowed to listen to the Qur'an while you're not paying full attention? Let's divide this into two scenarios.

The first scenario is that the Qur'an is being played and there is no intention to even listen to it, and there is in fact something disruptive going on: the ambience or the atmosphere that the Qur'an is being played in is not conducive; it's not meant to be listened to at all. And there are examples of this as well. Imam al-Qurtubi, for example, says that this verse came down because when the Quraysh would hear the Qur'an, they would raise their voices out of arrogance, and they would start blabbering away, saying anything, so that people would not listen to the Qur'an. So this verse came down telling the Muslims: don't follow that action. What was that action? To intentionally disrupt the recitation of the Qur'an, to do something obnoxious and rude. A'udhu billah, this is very dangerous; it could be a type of kufr even, if you intentionally want to disrespect the Qur'an by doing something of this nature.

But what if, again, you are not intentionally doing something, but still not wanting to pay attention? In this case, it is makruh or maybe even haram. The famous Hanbali scholar al-Buhuti says in Kashshaf al-Qina' that Ibn Aqil mentions that it is not allowed, it is haram, for the Qur'an to be recited in the marketplaces. What does he mean? Pause here. We're not talking about somebody wanting to recite and he's reciting of his own accord. We're talking about somebody who brings a qari' and says, "Hey, I want you to recite over here." We're talking about an intentional setup where the Qur'an is being recited and people are just talking away and transacting and whatnot. In other words, Imam al-Buhuti, one of the great Hanbali icons, is basically saying: don't have the Qur'an as background in the aswaq.

And sometimes we visit supermarkets in places around the world, and me personally, I don't like the fact that the Qur'an is being played in the entire marketplace. I know sometimes it feels good, and I understand that, but at the same time, in the bazaars and the supermarkets, I personally find this, again, like Imam al-Buhuti said: people are going to be negotiating, bargaining, they're arguing; things happen in the marketplace that might not necessarily be the best.

That having been said, I can see in some circumstances, if you're in a land where there are people of different ethnicities and cultures and faiths, and one shopkeeper has the Qur'an playing so that people know that this is, let's say, a shop that is owned by a Muslim, I can see a reason over there. But still, just to have the Qur'an playing for the sake of having the Qur'an playing in a massive supermarket or a bazaar or something of this nature, I find this to be not the best, because it's not the place that the Qur'an should be recited. There's an element that you're just doing something that maybe the majority of people are not interested in listening to.

This is the first scenario. And I would say that it is definitely best, as the default (I'm not saying in every scenario, as the default), to not intentionally play the Qur'an in an area where people are not really interested in listening to it. Now, that having been said, again, there are so many exceptions. Some of our scholars allowed the Qur'an to be played in a public area amongst non-Muslims that have never listened to the Qur'an, so that they can listen to something. Still, there are pros and cons, and again, each situation should be decided on a case-by-case basis. That's the first scenario. I would still say the default is more on the side of caution, to not play.

So let's give an example of the first scenario. You have the Qur'an playing, and you have a movie playing out loud as well in your own house. Why would you have the Qur'an playing and something happening on the television that is not appropriate, or music being played, and you are in control of both? You're the one who put the Qur'an on, and then somebody else, or maybe even you yourself, are watching there. Why would there be that? You don't want that clash to happen, do you? It's not something that is appropriate.

But your question is number two, the second scenario. And that is that you are wanting to listen to the Qur'an; that's why you're putting it on in the background. But you're also multitasking. That's the difference. Scenario one: there is no intention to listen to the Qur'an. It's just being played for noise or background; it's not something that is intended to be listened to. Scenario two: you are not able to listen to the Qur'an 100%, but you want to listen to it, and you're putting it on while you're multitasking. For example, you're cleaning the house, you're ironing the clothes, you're cooking, you're doing something, and the Qur'an is playing and you are listening to it, but you are also multitasking.

This scenario is separate from the first one. And in this scenario, yes, it is true, some of our modern scholars have discouraged it, including our teacher Shaykh Ibn Uthaymin, Allah yarhamuh, but there are many scholars that have allowed it. And I believe that, given the circumstances that we live in, the allowance seems to be the better of the two options, because your goal is to listen to it. Even if it's 50 percent, 40 percent, you're wanting to listen to it. And especially if you're memorizing, or you're listening to a surah that you love and you're just going over the meanings over and over again, the goal here is for the barakah, it is for the recitation. And you're putting it on while you're multitasking. Inshallah ta'ala, this does not contradict; there is no sin associated with it, because the alternative is nothing.

You see, here's the point: if you were to shut it off, what would you do? Astaghfirullah, some people would put on something that is no equivalent to the Qur'an as background, and we don't want that either. So given the circumstances, where people are turning away from the Book of Allah anyway, for a mother to put this on, and the children are toddlers, they're being raised to listen to the Qur'an: what a beautiful environment and ambience to be raised up in this manner.

And so in my humble opinion, and Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best, if it is the second scenario... Again, what is the first scenario? That it is being played and there's zero intention to listen to it. In this case, no, do not play it. Do not play it, because it is not appropriate to turn on the audio or the YouTube or the CD or the cassettes, whatever it is. Does anybody still use cassettes? I don't know. But anyway, I used to have hundreds of Qur'an cassettes; I had an entire section, hundreds, of all of the Qur'an. Anyway, that was back in the days of the 80s, and then the days of the CDs came, and then these days, nothing, it's just all online, subhanAllah. So my point is: you're going to put on the Qur'an and nobody wants to listen to it in the entire household, including you? No, that's not appropriate.

You put the Qur'an on, scenario two, and you are multitasking: one part of you is listening, the other part of you is cleaning, doing the chores. **Inshallah ta'ala, that is permissible, and it does not contradict the verse**, because there is a level of insat and a level of istima' going on. There's a level of "you want to listen," and a level of "okay, I want to put the Qur'an on because I want to listen to the meaning and the beauty of the Qur'an." So inshallah ta'ala, that is permissible, and Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best.
